attributes.title: Intermittent Weak Solutions of the 3D Euler Equations

body.value: In this talk, I will present a series of recent works, in part joint with H. Kwon, V. Giri, and V. Vicol. The common theme throughout is that the weak solutions we construct are intermittent; that is, they display deviations from the scaling laws predicted by Kolmogorov’s 1941 theory of turbulence. The techniques we have developed allow us to (1) prove a ”strong” version of Onsager’s famous conjecture, and (2) construct solutions to 3D Euler with well-defined helicity which is not conserved.

attributes.title: Quasi-convexity of harmonic map energy functions along Teichmüller geodesics and their asymptotic behavior

body.value: We show that the energy of harmonic maps f: M ----> S (Riemann surface varying along Teichmüller geodesic in Teichmüller space) is quasi-convex along Teichmüller geodesics generalizing previously known result about the length of closed geodesics. The asymptotic growth of the energy is t^2 along the Teichmüller geodesic determined by Jenkins-Strebel quadratic differentials. We determine the exact asymptotic constant using the energy of harmonic maps into  dual R-trees. This is a joint work with G. Zhang and X. Wan.

attributes.title: The Rényi entropy of the order of a random permutation

body.value:
The study of the order of a random permutation is a fundamental problem in probabilistic group theory. Its macroscopic behaviour is relatively well understood: a classical result of Erdős and Turán shows that the logarithm of the order is asymptotically normally distributed. Questions about its fine-scale distributional properties are more subtle due to the rich interaction with arithmetic. For instance, what is the most probable order of a random permutation of (1,...,n}, and with what probability does it occur? What is the probability that two independent random permutations have equal orders? The former question goes back to work of Erdős and Turán from the 1960s, while the latter was recently studied by Acan, Burnette, Eberhard, Schmutz and Thomas.

In this talk, I will present several results giving sharp asymptotic estimates for these questions. I will also explain how they relate to the unifying concept of Rényi entropy, and outline some of the ideas behind the proofs.

attributes.title: Regularity Methods in Combinatorics, Number Theory, and Computer Science

body.value: Understanding the structure of large graphs is a fundamental problem, as it can yield critical insights into topics ranging from the spread of diseases to how the brain works to patterns in the primes. Szemerédi's regularity lemma gives a rough structural result for all graphs. It is one of the most powerful tools in graph theory, with many applications in combinatorics, number theory, and computer science. Roughly speaking, it says that every graph can be partitioned into a small number of parts such that between almost all pairs of parts the graph is random-like. Variants of the regularity lemma have since been established with many further applications. In this talk, I will introduce the regularity method and its applications, and survey recent progress in understanding the quantitative aspects of these results.

attributes.title: Detection thresholds for random geometric graphs

body.value:
Random geometric graphs hide geometric structure inside an otherwise random-looking network: each vertex has a latent position on a high-dimensional sphere, and edges are formed between vertices that are sufficiently close. When can this hidden geometry be detected from the graph alone? In this talk, I will discuss recent results establishing indistinguishability from Erdős–Rényi random graphs above the conjectured sharp dimension threshold, whenever the average degree grows polynomially with the number of vertices.

This talk is based on joint work with Cheng Mao (Georgia Tech), Nike Sun (MIT), Yihong Wu (Yale), and Jialing Xu (Duke).

attributes.title: Topology of Lagrangians via open-closed string topology

body.value: The topology of Lagrangian submanifolds in the standard symplectic vector space C^n is a fundamental, yet poorly understood, problem in symplectic topology. A related question, known as Maslov class rigidity, concerns constraints on the Maslov classes of Lagrangian embeddings in C^n. I will describe a new approach to these problems based on ideas from open-closed string topology. As applications, I will present new results on these questions, extending classical theorems of Viterbo, Cieliebak–Mohnke, Fukaya, and Irie.

attributes.title: Higher-order paracontrolled calculus for geometric rough paths

body.value: We introduce the tools of higher-order paracontrolled calculus, developed originally in the works of Gubinelli-Imkeller-Perkowski and Bailleul-Bernicot, which provides a harmonic-analytic perspective on singular stochastic partial differential equations. We show how these methods can be adapted and extended to handle rough differential equations in a lower-regularity regime, and identify the necessary probabilistic data needed to give meaning to the equation. Part of our proof involves developing a general harmonic-analytic framework for proving commutator estimates which are necessary for expanding the solution to the equation, which is of independent interest.

attributes.title: Singularity Formation in 3D Euler and Nonuniqueness in Unforced 3D Navier–Stokes: Computer-Assisted Proofs

body.value: OpenAI's recently announced construction of a finite-time singularity for the Navier–Stokes equations relies crucially on $C^\infty$ external forcing. After brief remarks on this development, I will present two computer-assisted proofs for unforced incompressible flows. The first establishes finite-time, nearly self-similar blowup for the three-dimensional axisymmetric Euler equations with smooth, finite-energy initial data in a domain with boundary. It uses nonlinear stability around an approximate self-similar profile. The second establishes nonuniqueness of Leray–Hopf solutions to the unforced three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations from a common nonsmooth, finite-energy initial velocity. Key ingredients include the construction of an exact forward self-similar profile and rigorous verification of an unstable eigenmode of the associated linearized operator. Both analyses share a central strategy: decomposing the linearized operator into a coercive part, controlled through sharp functional-analytic estimates in weighted spaces, and a finite-rank perturbation, rigorously estimated with computer assistance. The talk will highlight the complementary roles of stability and instability and how numerical observations can be transformed into rigorous results. The Euler work is joint with Jiajie Chen, and the Navier–Stokes work is joint with Yixuan Wang and Changhe Yang.

attributes.title: The Exact Overlaps Conjecture on the Dimension of Self-Similar Measures

body.value:
Stationary measures are central objects in dynamics and probability. Self-similar measures are among the simplest examples of stationary measures, yet they are intricate to study. A similarity is a map from R^d to itself that uniformly scales distances and a self-similar measure is a stationary measure arising from the action of contracting similarities on R^d. The support of a self-similar measure is called a self-similar set, which is a central object in fractal geometry. Examples for self-similar sets are the Sierpinski triangle or the Menger sponge. The central question of interest for self-similar sets is to determine their Hausdorff dimension. More generally, one can also study the dimension of self-similar measures. 

The exact overlaps conjecture predicts a formula for the dimension of self-similar measures and therefore also of self-similar sets. I will present joint work with Samuel Kittle fully resolving the conjecture in dimension 1. Our proof was found with the help of GPT-6 Astra and published on the arXiv on the 7th of October, while the result was also contained in the announcement of OpenAI on the 6th of October as paper 148.

attributes.title: On filtration formula and nodal sets in min-max theory

body.value: There are many striking analogies between two areas of geometry: minimal surfaces theory (in particular min-max theory) and spectral geometry (in particular nodal geometry). These include asymptotic Weyl laws, multiplicity-one theorems, density results, and more. In this talk, I will discuss one approach to a rather philosophical question: What is the source of these similarities? Is there a deeper theory or principle that explains them? In particular, I will explain a counterexample to the asymptotic optimality conjecture of Marques and Neves, and how a less rigid notion of nodal sweepouts nevertheless recovers Gromov's volume spectrum. The talk is non-expert-friendly and assumes no background knowledge.

attributes.title: Bergman Distinguished Lecture: Large time behaviour in Fisher-KPP type equations

body.value:
The question addressed in this talk is the precise time asymptotic location of the level sets of the solutions of a class of partial differential equations that are usually referred to as "of the Fisher-KPP type", the acronym standing for Kolmogorov, Petrovskii, Piskunov. These equations arise in biology, ecology or population genetics; but also in probability, in the theory of branching random walks.

The sharpest information has, for a long time, come from probabilistic analyses. The goal of the talk is to present an alternative point of view which opens the way to the understanding of new situations, such as, for instance, nonlocal models, or models in heterogeneous media.

You can learn more about Professor Jean-Michel Roquejoffre on his website.

attributes.title: Quadratic cones as Einstein integrability loci

body.value: For every homogeneous quadratic scheme $Q\subseteq\mathbb A^N_{\mathbb Q}$ and every $n\ge3$, we construct a simply connected, smooth projective $n$-fold with a negative Kähler-Einstein metric, second Betti number two, and full holonomy $U(n)$, such that its space of essential infinitesimal Einstein deformations, together with its integrable directions, is stably complex-linearly equivalent to $(\mathbb C^N,Q(\mathbb C))$. Every infinitesimal Einstein deformation extends to second order, and extension to third order is equivalent to integrability. Affine cones over arbitrary projective varieties defined over $\mathbb Q$, in suitable embeddings, therefore admit such realizations.

attributes.title: Hikita conjecture for quiver gauge theories

body.value: Hikita conjecture predicts a ring isomorphism between the cohomology ring of a symplectic resolution $\tilde X$ of a symplectic variety $X$ and the coordinate ring of the scheme theoretic fixed points in the symplectic dual variety $X^\vee$. Open AI announced a proof of this conjecture on Oct. 6 when $X$ is a quiver variety and $X^\vee$ is the corresponding Coulomb branch. I will explain symplectic duality, the statement of Hikita conjecture, and a few key points of Open AI proof.

attributes.title: The phase diagram of two-layer neural networks

body.value:
One of the most remarkable properties of modern AI systems is to learn and often memorize large training sets and yet generalize well to unseen data.

I will give an overview of work carried out over the past several years to undestand the interplay of overfitting and generalization in simple two layer networks.

attributes.title: Bounded gaps between primes via APs with partly smooth moduli

body.value: Building on Yitang Zhang's work on bounded gaps between primes, the Polymath project showed that there are infinitely many prime gaps which are no larger than 246. In this talk I will discuss how the Bombieri-Vinogradov theorem can be combined with newer equidistribution estimates for primes in APs to obtain an improvement on Polymath's result. The key ingredient is a new choice of support for the functions appearing in the corresponding optimization problem for the GPY sieve. To choose this support, we produce various equidistribution conditions for moduli with a large smooth factor, and reduce the calculation of relevant integrals to matrix multiplication and recursion.

body.value: In this talk, we consider the upper-tail large deviations of intersections of Brownian motions. Apart from intrinsic interest, these quantities are also closely related to the parabolic Anderson model via the Feynman-Kac formula. We prove that the occupation measures of Brownian motions conditioned to have large intersections converge weakly, up to spatial shifts, to the measure whose density is the square of an optimizer of the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality. The key tools are a compactification of the weak topology and an exponentially good approximation of the Brownian occupation measure.

attributes.title: Capacities on dynamically convex toric domains and embedding obstructions

body.value: In this talk, I will introduce a sequence of symplectic capacities defined using cylindrical contact homology (CCH), based on unpublished work of Michael Hutchings and cobordism maps constructed by Hutchings and Jo Nelson. I will explain how topological constraints on holomorphic cylinders rule out certain terms in the CCH differential, while known capacity computations and cobordism maps force other terms to be nonzero. These arguments lead to explicit formulas for the differential and the capacities of four-dimensional monotone toric domains. I will conclude with examples of new symplectic embedding obstructions between monotone toric domains and discuss blind spots of CCH capacities.

attributes.title: Agentic AI for mathematical reasoning and verification

body.value: Well-designed agentic harnesses can substantially extend the capabilities of foundation models in mathematical reasoning and verification. I will illustrate this through case studies of three provers (Rethlas, Danus, and Pharos) and one verifier (OSVerify). I will also discuss the design philosophy behind these systems from a mathematician's perspective, and directions for future work.

attributes.title: Sturmian discrete and metric graphs - appearance and absence of gaps.

body.value: We study the spectra of Sturmian Schroedinger operators on graphs (either metric or discrete).A Sturmian sequence is an aperiodic sequence which is determined by an irrational frequency.These sequences are used to form aperiodic graph structures.We consider the integrated density of states (IDS) for Schroedinger operators on such graphs.The gap labelling theory predicts all the possible gaps in the spectra of these operators.We explicitly compute the gap labels; we show which gaps appear in the spectrum and which are absent, and why.The talk is based on joint works with Siegfried Beckus, Raphael Loewy and Gilad Sofer.

body.value: Until recently it was unknown whether every knotted projective plane in S^4 decomposes as a connected sum of a "trivial" projective plane and a knotted 2-sphere (the Kinoshita Conjecture). I'll talk about some classic constructions of knotted surfaces and how they motivated us to find an irreducible projective plane. This is joint work with Mark Hughes, Seungwon Kim, and Gheehyun Nahm.

The goal of the talk is to explore the corrections beyond the linear term.

attributes.title: A quasipolynomial inverse theorem for the U^k(F_p^n) norm in the high characteristic

body.value: The inverse theory for Gowers uniformity norms is one of the central topics in additive combinatorics and one of the most important aspects of the theory is the question of bounds. In this talk, I will discuss a recent work, which proves a quasipolynomial inverse theorem for $mathsf{U}^k$ norm in $\mathbb{F}_p^n$ in the case of high characteristic (meaning $p \geq k$). I will discuss the key ingredients of the argument: the abstract Balog-Szemerédi-Gowers theorem, algebraic regularity method and the theory of multilinear maps defined on multilinear varieties. Along the way, I will highlight the differences from previous works in the inverse theory of uniformity norms.

attributes.title: How to construct a quantum Markov chain

body.value: Classical Markov chains and Monte Carlo methods have driven major advances in statistical physics, probability, and modern computation. In this talk, I will present a general construction of quantum Markov chains that provides both a rigorous quantum algorithmic framework for sampling Gibbs states and a physically consistent dynamical model of thermalization in noncommutative many-body quantum systems. Together, these perspectives reveal new mathematical challenges whose resolution could unlock useful early applications of quantum computers.

body.value:
If planning to attend, please submit an RSVP here.

The Stanford Mathematics Research Center presents Surprises from rubbing the wrong way, a lecture given by Tadashi Tokieda, Professor of Mathematics at Stanford University, as part of the MRC Public Lecture series.

Friction, stickiness, jamming . . . Don’t we frown on these conditions as spoilers of life? This lecture, however, will perform baffling experiments that pop out of these conditions, and probe their subtle physics via simple mathematics. You’ll be able to enjoy many of the experiments with friends and family as easy magic.

Tadashi Tokieda is starting his 10th year as a member of the Stanford math department, after vagabonding across careers — painter, philologist, precarious plumber, physicist. He likes to collect counter‑intuitive phenomena which he discovers, designs, or learns about from others, and to share them in outreach, e.g. via the YouTube channel Numberphile. T^2 spoke in that capacity at the quadrennial International Congress of Mathematicians 2018, 2022, 2026.

This lecture is free and open to the public.

See the full event poster here.

You can find more information about speaker Tadashi Tokieda on the Stanford Math Department website.

attributes.title: Recent progress in Bridgeland stability conditions

body.value: Bridgeland stability conditions provide a powerful tool for studying complexes of coherent sheaves on algebraic varieties. I will discuss some recent progress on their existence, moduli spaces of stable objects, Bogomolov-type inequalities, and related applications.

attributes.title: Geometric configurations in sparse subsets of the integer lattice

body.value:
We study the problem of how dense a subset of the integer lattice can be without containing a similar copy of a given simplex. We give an overview of a functional analytic approach, that combines techniques of analytic number theory, the geometry of numbers and purely analytic tools, leading to power-saving bounds. Time permitting, we plan to discuss some extensions, such as configurations consisting of a simplex together with its barycentre - a geometric analogue of Roth’s theorem on three term arithmetic progressions.

This is joint work with Andrew Lott and Nagendar Reddy Ponagandla.

attributes.title: Oscillation of graph eigenfunctions and its applications

body.value: Oscillation theory, originally due to Sturm, seeks to connect the number of sign changes of an eigenfunction of a self-adjoint operator to the label k of the corresponding eigenvalue.  Its applications run in both directions: knowing k, one may wish to estimate the zero set, or the topology of its complement, useful in clustering and partitioning problems.  Conversely, knowing an eigenvector (and thus the number of its sign changes), one may want to determine if it ist he ground state, useful in the linear stability analysis of solutions to nonlinear equations.Within the setting of generalized graph Laplacians, Fiedler's theorem says that the k-th eigenvector of a tree (a graph without cycles) changes sign across exactly k-1 edges.  We present a formula for the number of sign changes on a general graph, which attributes the excess sign changes to the cycles in the graph and their intersections.This result has many interesting connections.  First, it allows one to derive a simple formula for the effective mass tensor of a particular class of crystals (periodic lattices), namely the maximal abelian covers of finite graphs.  Second, it can be used to efficiently determine stability of a stationary solution on a coupled oscillator network, such as the non-uniform Kuramoto model for the synchronization of a network of electrical oscillators.  Finally, the determinant of the matrix which determines the excess sign changes is closely related to the graph's Kirchhoff polynomial (which counts the weighted spanning trees), hinting at connections to both Feynman amplitudes and matroids. Based on a joint work with Jared Bronski (UI Urbana-Champaign) and Mark Goresky (IAS Princeton).

attributes.title: Support recovery of diffusion models under the manifold hypothesis

body.value: We study diffusion models under the manifold hypothesis with possibly large score estimation and discretization errors, and show that while they may not exactly recover the data distribution, they will recover the support (or data manifold). In continuous time, we show that even if the relative score estimation error is fixed (and not necessarily vanishing), then the rate at which the process approaches the support is $O(\sqrt{(T-t)|\log(T-t)|})$ as~$t \to T$, where~$T$ is the final time. In discrete time, we use geometric time steps with a fixed (non-vanishing) ratio and show that with a fixed relative score estimation error, the process approaches the data manifold exponentially with the number of iterations. The proof relies on controlling a Gaussian measure of a neighborhood of the cut-locus of the data manifold, which, in turn, uses arguments from computational real algebraic geometry. This is a joint work with A. Alieva, G. Iyer and A. Novikov.
